At Ista, the exiled Oldtimer leader T'kul is dead by F'lar's hand after his bronze died attempting a queen's mating flight, which ends the exiled Weyr as a threat, and D'ram, recovered from the past, takes charge in the south. Jaxom's own question is settled last: having flown Thread with Ruth in the open, recovered the stolen queen egg, found D'ram and helped uncover the ancient settlement, he is confirmed as Lord Holder of Ruatha while remaining Ruth's rider, an arrangement the holds and the Weyrs both accept because he has made it impossible to argue with. He takes Sharra as his lady over her brother Toric's objections. Toric's ambitions in the south, and the question of what the buried settlement will eventually tell Pern about itself, are left open.
recaps.in_short: Jaxom, Lord Holder of Ruatha and rider of the undersized white dragon Ruth, is allowed to be neither a proper Lord nor a proper dragonrider, and secretly trains Ruth to fly between and to flame Thread. When the riders exiled to the Southern Continent steal a queen egg from Benden's Hatching Ground and bring the Weyrs to the edge of war, Jaxom uses Ruth's unique certainty about time and place to take it back and return it unseen. He falls dangerously ill afterwards and is sent to a southern cove to recover, where the healer Sharra, the harpers Menolly and Piemur and the wider south open up a life nobody is managing for him. He locates the retired Weyrleader D'ram in the past when no other dragon could; at Ista the exiled leader T'kul loses his dragon, attacks F'lar and is killed, and Masterharper Robinton survives a heart attack and is retired to a hold built at Jaxom's cove. Following memories carried by fire lizards, the group uncovers the buried settlement of Pern's first colonists. Jaxom is confirmed as Lord of Ruatha, keeps Ruth, and takes Sharra as his lady.

recaps.text: Pern is periodically scoured by Thread, a spore that falls from a wandering neighbouring planet and devours anything living. The defence is dragons, telepathically bonded for life to their riders, flying from mountain Weyrs and flaming Thread out of the air. In Dragonflight, after four hundred Turns without a Fall, only Benden Weyr remained occupied. The bronze rider F'lar found Lessa, the last heir of Ruatha Hold, hiding as a drudge under the conqueror Fax, killed Fax, and became Weyrleader when Lessa's queen Ramoth flew to mate. Thread returned, Benden's dragons were far too few, and Lessa rode Ramoth four hundred Turns into the past to bring Pern's five abandoned Weyrs forward in time, saving the planet and importing thousands of riders raised four centuries earlier. In Dragonquest, those Oldtimer riders proved unable to accept a Pern where holds and crafts no longer obeyed the Weyrs without question. Fire lizards, small telepathic cousins of dragons, were discovered and spread across Pern; two queen dragons fought and died, leaving Brekke dragonless; F'nor's attempt to fly to the Red Star ended any hope of attacking Thread at its source, while grubs found in the Southern Continent proved able to destroy Thread in the soil. F'lar finally defeated the Oldtimer leader T'ron in a duel and exiled the irreconcilable riders to the south. At the Hatching that followed, Jaxom, the boy Lord Holder of Ruatha, opened an undersized egg and Impressed the white dragon Ruth.

Turns on, Jaxom is in his teens, Lord Holder of Ruatha in title while his warder Lytol governs, and rider of a dragon nobody knows how to classify. Ruth is full grown at roughly half the size of an ordinary dragon, white, healthy and clever, and the Weyrs have quietly decided he is a pet: not to be flown against Thread, not expected ever to rise to mate, and not to be taken seriously. Jaxom is caught in the same judgement from the other side. The Lord Holders will not risk Ruatha's heir in a Fall; Benden will not let a hold's Lord fly in a wing. So he is taught hold management, drilled on his responsibilities and kept out of the sky, while the boys he trained beside go to the Weyrs. He also begins to notice something about his dragon that no Record describes: Ruth is never disoriented, never uncertain, and always knows precisely where and when he is, which is exactly the sense that ordinary dragons lose when they travel between times.

Jaxom decides that if nobody will train Ruth, he will do it himself, and teaches him to fly between in secret, working from the visual references a rider must hold in mind to travel. Then Pern's balance breaks: the riders exiled to the Southern Continent, aging and without a queen of breeding age to keep their Weyr alive, steal a queen egg from Benden's Hatching Ground. Benden is prepared to go to war over it, the northern Weyrs would be fighting each other in the middle of a Pass, and no ordinary dragon can be sent to search the south without being seen. Jaxom realizes that Ruth's certainty about time makes them the one pair on Pern who could take the egg back without being caught. They go, find the egg among the exiles, and return it to Benden's sands almost unnoticed, which averts the war. Jaxom cannot claim what he has done, because admitting it would mean admitting everything else he has been doing with Ruth.

The egg is back and the crisis passes, but the secret sits badly with Jaxom, and only a handful of people ever learn the truth of it. N'ton, the Fort Weyrleader, works out enough of what Ruth can do to become an ally rather than an obstacle, and quietly helps Jaxom train instead of reporting him. Jaxom pushes further: if Ruth can fly between, he can chew firestone and flame, and Jaxom sets about teaching him. Between hold duties, his own frustration at being managed, and a young woman named Corana at a small holding on Ruathan land, he is living three separate lives, none of which the Lords or the Weyrs would sanction. Ruth, meanwhile, is followed everywhere by fire lizards, who treat him with a deference they show no other dragon, and whose fragmentary shared memories are stranger than anyone has bothered to examine.

Jaxom takes Ruth into Threadfall, and the pair prove they can fight, though the manner of it can no longer be hidden. Shortly afterwards Jaxom collapses with firehead, a fever that leaves him weak and disoriented for a long time, and the healers order him out of the northern winter. He is sent to convalesce at a quiet cove on the Southern Continent, where the climate does the work no medicine can. There he is nursed by Sharra, a healer from Southern Hold, and joined by the harpers Menolly and Piemur, with Brekke and F'nor keeping an eye on all of them. For the first time in his life nobody is managing Jaxom's future for him. He recovers slowly, swims, explores the coast with Ruth, and falls in love with Sharra, while the south itself, unmapped and enormous, starts to look like the answer to a question the north has not asked.

D'ram, the Istan Weyrleader, loses his Weyrwoman and disappears rather than preside over the succession, leaving Ista leaderless in the middle of a Pass. Because only Ruth can fix a person's exact time as well as place, Jaxom is the one who finds him, in an earlier Turn at a southern cove, and persuades him to come back. Ista's queen then rises to mate, and T'kul, leader of the exiled riders, brings his aged bronze north to fly her. The dragon dies in the attempt. T'kul, dragonless and beyond reason, attacks F'lar, and F'lar kills him, which effectively ends the exiled Weyr as a threat. In the same crisis Masterharper Robinton suffers a heart attack and very nearly dies. He survives, is forbidden to go on as he has, and D'ram takes on the southern responsibility. A hold is built for Robinton's retirement at the cove where Jaxom convalesced, so that Pern's most useful man can be kept alive and still be talked to.

With Robinton installed at Cove Hold and a standing company of harpers, riders and holders around him, the southern coast becomes the centre of Pern's curiosity rather than its politics. Ruth's peculiar hold over fire lizards turns out to matter: the creatures carry inherited images from far further back than any Record, among them a mountain that burned and people who went away. Piemur's Turns of exploring the south, Ruth's certainty about place, and Robinton's willingness to take a fire lizard's memory as evidence combine into an actual search. Jaxom, now openly flying Thread with Ruth and no longer pretending otherwise, spends his time between Ruatha's business, Sharra, and the hunt. On a high plateau inland the group finds regular shapes under a deep layer of old volcanic ash, and starts to dig.

What they uncover is the settlement of Pern's first people: buildings of stone and unfamiliar metal, buried when the mountain erupted and abandoned by ancestors who left the site and, over the centuries, lost even the memory of it. It is the first physical proof that Pern's inhabitants came from somewhere else and once possessed things the crafts cannot now make, and it changes what Pern can ask about itself. Around that discovery everything else settles. T'kul is dead and the exiled Weyr finished; D'ram holds the south for the Weyrs; Robinton is alive at Cove Hold with more than enough to occupy him; Toric of Southern Hold is quietly counting how much of the continent he can claim before the north notices. Jaxom's own status, unresolved for the whole book, is resolved by what he has done rather than by anyone's ruling: he is confirmed as Lord Holder of Ruatha and remains Ruth's rider, flying Thread with the Weyrs, the first man on Pern to hold both places at once. He takes Sharra as his lady, over her brother's objections, and Ruatha has a Lord again.

characters.description: The book's narrator, writing from Bangalore to the visiting Chinese premier. Born without a settled name in the village of Laxmangarh, he is officially called Balram Halwai and is nicknamed the White Tiger by a school inspector who notices his intelligence. Now a self-made entrepreneur, he promises to explain how a poor servant became a wealthy businessman.
characters.name: Balram Halwai

characters.description: The younger son of a wealthy landlord family from Laxmangarh and Balram's principal employer. Recently returned from the United States, he appears gentler and less comfortable with feudal privilege than his relatives, though he still benefits from their money and power.
characters.name: Mr. Ashok

characters.description: Ashok's wife, raised in India but strongly attached to the life the couple had in the United States. Independent and impatient with his family's customs, she dislikes their return to India and the restrictions surrounding her as a wealthy daughter-in-law.
characters.name: Pinky Madam

characters.description: Ashok's older brother, a sharp and suspicious manager of the family's interests. He monitors servants closely and treats bribery, household discipline, and the protection of family wealth as practical business.
characters.name: Mukesh Sir

characters.description: Ashok and Mukesh's father, one of the powerful landlords who dominate Balram's home village. His family profits from coal and other enterprises, collecting wealth through intimidation, political influence, and control over local people.
characters.name: The Stork

characters.description: Balram's commanding grandmother and the authority within his extended family. She controls family earnings and decisions, expects obedience from younger relatives, and presses Balram to send his wages home.
characters.name: Kusum

characters.description: Balram's older brother, who works alongside him after poverty forces both boys out of school. More resigned to family duty than Balram, he helps arrange Balram's driving lessons and employment.
characters.name: Kishan

characters.description: Balram's father, a poor rickshaw puller who wants at least one son to receive the education denied to him. Hard labor and illness leave him unable to protect that hope from the family's immediate need for income.
characters.name: Vikram Halwai

characters.description: The Stork family's senior driver when Balram joins the household. Experienced and outwardly secure in his position, he becomes Balram's rival for the preferred driving assignments.
characters.name: Ram Persad

characters.description: A driver and informal fixer recognizable by patches of vitiligo around his mouth. He teaches Balram how Delhi's chauffeurs obtain supplies, information, entertainment, and illicit opportunities while waiting for their employers.
characters.name: Vitiligo-Lips

characters.description: A powerful populist politician whose party controls the Darkness, including Laxmangarh. He presents himself as a champion of the poor while participating in the networks of bribery and patronage used by wealthy families.
characters.name: The Great Socialist

characters.description: A young nephew from Balram's extended family sent from the village to live with him in Delhi. His arrival makes Balram responsible for a child just as Balram is contemplating a decisive break with his employers and family obligations.
characters.name: Dharam

characters.description: The Chinese premier to whom Balram addresses his series of letters after hearing that he will visit Bangalore to learn about Indian entrepreneurship. He does not participate directly in Balram's story but provides its imagined audience.
characters.name: Wen Jiabao

recaps.ending: Balram decides that the red bag of bribe money in Ashok's car is his route out of servitude. After sending a warning letter home, he drives Ashok to a secluded area, kills him with a broken bottle, takes the money, and flees Delhi with his young nephew Dharam. He assumes that the Stork's family will retaliate against his relatives in Laxmangarh, though he never confirms their fate. In Bangalore he adopts the name Ashok Sharma, uses part of the stolen money to bribe the police, and builds a taxi company serving call-center workers. When one of his drivers kills a boy in an accident, Balram pays and pressures the bereaved family while protecting the business, repeating the methods of the powerful men he escaped. He nonetheless regards his company and care for Dharam as a freer life. He ends his letters convinced that the murder was the price of becoming an entrepreneur and imagining further business success.
recaps.in_short: Balram Halwai, the son of a poor rickshaw puller in rural India, writes to China's premier from Bangalore to explain his rise as an entrepreneur. Intelligent but removed from school, Balram becomes a chauffeur for the wealthy Stork family and drives the American-returned Ashok and his wife Pinky in Delhi. Service exposes him to two Indias: the protected world of malls, apartments, political influence, and bribes, and the precarious lives of servants whose families help keep them obedient. After Pinky kills a child in a road accident, Balram is prepared as the family's scapegoat, though no charge follows. Pinky leaves, Ashok becomes increasingly corrupt and isolated, and Balram turns from admiring him to planning escape. He murders Ashok, steals a bag of bribe money, and flees with his nephew Dharam. In Bangalore, using the name Ashok Sharma, Balram bribes officials and creates a successful taxi fleet. His freedom rests on violence and on adopting many practices of the class he once served.

recaps.text: Writing over several nights to Chinese premier Wen Jiabao, Bangalore businessman Balram Halwai begins explaining how he escaped poverty. He grew up in Laxmangarh, a village in the impoverished region he calls the Darkness, where four landlords dominate local life. A teacher gave the nameless boy the name Balram, and a visiting inspector called him a rare white tiger because of his intelligence. Although promised further schooling, Balram was sent to work in a tea shop so his family could repay debts. His father, a rickshaw puller who wanted a better future for him, died of tuberculosis after receiving little effective medical care. Determined not to remain trapped, Balram learns to drive and gains employment with the Stork's wealthy family. He becomes their second driver, serving the Stork's sons Ashok and Mukesh and Ashok's wife Pinky. Balram discovers that the senior driver, Ram Persad, is concealing his Muslim identity and uses the information to force him out, winning the preferred driver's position and a transfer to Delhi.

Balram drives Ashok and Pinky through Delhi, observing how servants wait in basements while their employers move through luxury hotels, malls, and government offices. Ashok's family makes regular payments to politicians to protect its coal interests. Ashok seems personally kinder than Mukesh and uneasy about corruption, but he continues to participate in the system that enriches him. Pinky resents India and her husband's family. On her birthday she becomes drunk, insists on driving, and hits a child in the road before leaving the scene. The family prepares Balram to accept legal responsibility, reminding him that his relatives in Laxmangarh are vulnerable to retaliation. Balram signs a confession he cannot read freely, but the police never pursue a case because no victim's family comes forward. The episode clarifies what his apparent closeness to Ashok is worth: when danger threatens the employers, the servant is expendable.

Pinky gives Balram money, leaves Ashok, and returns to the United States. Ashok grows lonely and relies more heavily on Balram, yet the reduced distance between them does not make them equals. Balram watches Ashok carry large bribes, drink, pursue women, and gradually lose the scruples he brought back from America. Through other drivers and his own secret excursions, Balram learns how servants exploit small openings in their employers' routines, but he also describes the larger restraint as a rooster coop: fear for one's family keeps servants from rebelling even when escape seems possible. His resentment intensifies as he compares the money passing through his car with the life available to him. When Kusum sends his young nephew Dharam to Delhi, Balram must consider that any move against Ashok may bring punishment upon both the boy and the family back home. Nevertheless, he begins weighing the red bag of bribe money as the means to a new identity.

Balram decides to break out of servitude despite the likely cost to his family. After composing a warning for Kusum, he drives Ashok with a large bag of cash intended for politicians. In a secluded place he pretends the car has a problem, lures Ashok out, and kills him with a broken liquor bottle. Balram takes the money and escapes Delhi with Dharam. He believes the Stork's family will murder his relatives in revenge, though he does not learn exactly what happened. In Bangalore, Balram adopts the name Ashok Sharma and uses bribes to establish a taxi fleet serving call centers, eventually becoming a prosperous employer. When one of his drivers kills a boy, Balram protects the company by paying the family and using police influence, behaving much like the powerful people he condemns. He treats his drivers comparatively well and accepts responsibility for Dharam's future, but feels no remorse for Ashok's murder. He closes his account imagining further ventures and insisting that his crime made his independent life possible.

characters.description: A mortal in her late teens who serves as seneschal to the High King of Elfhame and, in secret, rules through him: Cardan is bound by oath to obey her for a year and a day, and the commands he gives at court are hers. She holds power nobody has agreed to give her and keeps it with spycraft, poison tolerance and nerve, while the clock on the oath runs down and she cannot tell a single person why she is so anxious about the date.
characters.name: Jude Duarte

characters.description: The youngest son of the murdered High King, crowned through Jude's manoeuvring and bound to do as she says for a year and a day. He wears the crown as a provocation, fills his days with drink and revels, mocks the office and the girl holding his leash, and occasionally shows a sharper political instinct than anyone expects of him. What he actually wants from Jude is impossible to read.
characters.name: Cardan

characters.description: Jude's twin, engaged to Locke and preparing for the wedding that will finally give her the settled place in Faerie she has always wanted. The sisters are on speaking terms again but not repaired; Taryn resents both Jude's refusal to live quietly and the danger she keeps walking into.
characters.name: Taryn Duarte

characters.description: Jude's adoptive father, the redcap general who backed Balekin's coup and lost. Stripped of his command and kept away from the throne, he is still the most dangerous soldier in Elfhame and still speaks to Jude as a father would. He is patient, he wants a war, and he is working out who is really giving the orders.
characters.name: Madoc

characters.description: A green-skinned hob and the most seasoned of the spies of the Court of Shadows, now working for Jude. He handles locks, thefts and the practical business of running informants, and he is candid with her about how badly her position could go wrong.
characters.name: The Roach

characters.description: The explosives expert of the Court of Shadows, white-haired and unflappable, one of the few people who knows exactly what Jude is doing and helps her do it. She is loyal, practical, and better company than anyone else Jude works with.
characters.name: The Bomb

characters.description: Taryn's betrothed, a fey lord who once courted both Duarte sisters at the same time for his own entertainment. Cardan appoints him Master of Revels, which gives him a court office and licence to stage entertainments, and he uses it to arrange situations that produce the reactions he enjoys watching.
characters.name: Locke

characters.description: The eldest Duarte sister, half fey, living in the human world with her mortal girlfriend and raising Oak there. She has the life away from Faerie she always wanted and no intention of returning, and she is increasingly unwilling to keep lying to Heather about what she is.
characters.name: Vivienne

characters.description: Vivi's mortal girlfriend in the human world, who shares a flat with her and the children and knows nothing about Faerie. She is warm, ordinary and entirely unprepared for the truth about the family she has attached herself to.
characters.name: Heather

characters.description: Jude's small half-brother, secretly the son of the murdered Prince Dain and therefore the true heir of the blood, growing up in the human world where nobody can crown him. He is settling happily into a mortal childhood, which complicates every plan to bring him back.
characters.name: Oak

characters.description: Madoc's fey wife and Oak's mother, who hid the boy's parentage for years and now lives apart from her son. She has never trusted Jude, and she is the person with the most to lose from any move Madoc makes.
characters.name: Oriana

characters.description: Princess of the Undersea, Cardan's former sweetheart and her mother's envoy to the High Court. She despises mortals as thoroughly as ever, still considers Cardan hers, and carries the growing impatience of a sea power that the land cannot afford to fight.
characters.name: Nicasia

characters.description: Cardan's eldest brother, who murdered their father and most of their family to seize a crown he never got to wear, now held prisoner in the Tower of Forgetting. Confinement has not humbled him: he is composed, contemptuous, and evidently still able to get messages out of his cell.
characters.name: Prince Balekin

characters.description: Queen of the Undersea and Nicasia's mother, ruler of the one power in the world that Elfhame cannot easily fight. She is negotiating terms with the new High King and treats her own patience as a resource to be spent for advantage.
characters.name: Queen Orlagh

recaps.ending: Madoc finally moves against the throne in the open, backed by soldiers and by allies gathered while the court was distracted, and demands that Cardan give up the crown. With Jude's year and a day almost spent and a claim through the child heir Oak the obvious way for Madoc to legitimise a seizure, Cardan and Jude marry in front of the court. The marriage makes Jude High Queen of Elfhame, wrecking Madoc's plan, since there is now a crowned consort in the way of any regency. It is the moment Jude's hidden power becomes real and public rather than a secret held by an oath. Cardan's next act, moments later and in front of everyone, is to exile her: he banishes Jude from Faerie, and a royal command is not something she can refuse. She is put out into the mortal world, forbidden to return, cut off from the court, her spies and her brother's future, and with no explanation of whether the betrayal was calculation, revenge for the leash she kept him on, or something else entirely. Madoc remains at large with his forces intact, the Undersea has its treaty and Balekin, and the High Queen of Elfhame is stranded in the human world.
recaps.in_short: Five months after crowning Cardan, Jude Duarte runs Elfhame from behind the throne as his seneschal, holding him to an oath that expires after a year and a day. She fends off assassins, the scheming of her exiled adoptive father Madoc, and the demands of Queen Orlagh of the Undersea, whose envoy is Cardan's former sweetheart Nicasia, while trying to keep her secret from a court that would kill a mortal for far less. Taryn marries Locke, Cardan makes Locke Master of Revels, and Jude's grip on both the king and the realm slowly loosens. Jude is seized by the Undersea and held beneath the water until Cardan buys her back with a treaty and the prisoner Balekin. Back at court, with the oath nearly expired and Madoc's rebellion breaking into the open, Cardan and Jude marry, making her High Queen and destroying Madoc's claim to a regency. Then, in front of the assembled court, Cardan exiles her to the mortal world, and she cannot disobey.

recaps.text: Previously, in The Cruel Prince: the mortal twins Jude and Taryn Duarte were taken into Faerie as children by Madoc, the redcap general who had killed their mother, once his wife, and her human husband. Raised in his household with their half-fey sister Vivienne, they were despised by the fey gentry, above all by Prince Cardan and his companions. Wanting power of her own, Jude swore herself to Prince Dain as a spy and joined his Court of Shadows, killed Valerian when he attacked her, and lost her sister's trust when she discovered Locke had been courting both twins at once with Taryn's knowledge. At the coronation, Prince Balekin murdered the High King and most of his heirs, with Madoc as his ally, and Dain was shot by the Ghost, Balekin's man inside the Court of Shadows. Jude captured Cardan, the last heir who could pass the crown, and learned that her small brother Oak was secretly Dain's son and the true heir Madoc intended to rule through. She put Cardan on the throne instead, in exchange for his oath to obey her for a year and a day, saw Balekin imprisoned and Madoc stripped of his command, and sent Oak to the human world to be raised by Vivi. Taryn stayed behind, engaged to Locke.

Five months into Cardan's reign, Jude serves as his seneschal, which lets a mortal stand beside the throne without anyone asking why the High King listens to her. In private she is the one ruling: the oath binds Cardan to obey her, and she uses it to keep him from wrecking the crown he never wanted. The court is dangerous ground. The Living Council resents her, the gentry resent her more, Cardan drinks and holds revels and needles her at every opportunity, and he appoints Locke, now Taryn's betrothed, as Master of Revels over Jude's objection. Balekin sits in the Tower of Forgetting, unrepentant. Madoc, out of office but not out of power, watches the palace and asks pointed questions. The Undersea is pressing for terms, with Queen Orlagh's daughter Nicasia at court to make the pressure felt. Oak is safe in the human world with Vivi and her girlfriend Heather, and Jude means to keep him there for years yet. She has the Court of Shadows, an income of secrets, and a deadline she has told no one about.

Jude's position starts to cost more than it pays. There are attempts on her life and on Cardan's, and it becomes clear that someone inside the palace is working for an enemy. She questions Balekin in his cell and learns that his imprisonment has not cut him off from correspondents, and that his interest in the Undersea is not idle. Orlagh's demands harden, and Nicasia makes plain that a treaty on the sea's terms is the price of peace. Jude keeps the realm running by exhausting herself: reading reports, buying informants, managing Cardan in public and arguing with him in private, while the antagonism between them turns into something neither will name. She visits the human world to see Oak, and finds Vivi's relationship with Heather strained by everything Vivi has not told her. Meanwhile Madoc, courteous and unhurried, keeps testing where the real authority in Elfhame sits.

Taryn marries Locke, and the wedding brings the whole court together, including Madoc, who uses the occasion for his own purposes. The sisters' truce holds only as long as neither says what she means. Jude's control of Cardan grows more precarious as the year and a day nears its end and she has no plan for what follows; her authority depends entirely on an oath that will simply stop. Cardan, for his part, has begun ruling in ways Jude did not instruct, and their relationship shifts from hostility to something intimate that neither of them trusts. The Undersea's pressure and the palace's internal treachery converge, and Jude realises that Madoc knows more about how the throne is really being run than he should.

Jude is seized by the Undersea and taken beneath the water, where she is held for a long stretch, kept alive by enchantment and deliberately broken down by her captors, with Nicasia among them. She endures it, gives up nothing useful, and comes back harder and more frightened than she will admit. Her release is bought at a price: a treaty with Queen Orlagh on terms the land would rather not have accepted, and the handing over of Balekin, who leaves the Tower of Forgetting to become Elfhame's ambassador to the Undersea, a punishment that looks a great deal like a promotion. Jude returns to a court that has kept moving without her, an oath nearly expired, and a general who has spent her absence preparing.

Back at the palace, the secret that has held Elfhame together comes apart. Madoc learns that it is Jude, not Cardan, who has been ruling, and he moves from testing to acting, gathering soldiers and allies for a claim of his own with the child heir Oak as his justification. Jude tries to hold her position with the days on the oath running out, weighing whether to force one last binding on Cardan, whether to bring Oak home, and whether Cardan can be trusted at all once he is free. Her spies confirm that Madoc's rebellion is real and close, and that the court will not defend a mortal seneschal. Cardan, meanwhile, is no longer behaving like a man being led.

Madoc moves openly against the throne, demanding that Cardan give up the crown, with force behind the demand and a regency for Oak as his path to legitimacy. Cardan and Jude counter it by marrying in front of the court: the marriage makes Jude High Queen of Elfhame, which leaves no room for a regent and turns her hidden power into a public, permanent fact. Then, moments after the ceremony, Cardan exiles her. He banishes Jude from Faerie before the assembled court, and because it is a royal command she cannot refuse it. She is put out into the mortal world, barred from returning, separated from her spies, her sister and her brother, and given no reason for any of it. Madoc remains in the field with his army, the Undersea has its treaty and Balekin, and the newly crowned High Queen of Elfhame is stranded among humans with no way home.

characters.description: The eldest Baudelaire, a fourteen-year-old inventor who ties back her hair to think and improvises devices to get her family out of danger. Having survived Count Olaf twice and lost two guardians, she remains the steady, protective leader of her younger siblings as they are moved to yet another home.
characters.name: Violet Baudelaire

characters.description: The middle Baudelaire, a twelve-year-old with glasses who reads voraciously and recalls what he learns. His knowledge has repeatedly saved the children, and he stays alert for Count Olaf, whom he no longer trusts any disguise to hide.
characters.name: Klaus Baudelaire

characters.description: The baby of the family, who speaks in short exclamations her siblings understand and whose four sharp teeth can bite through almost anything. Small but determined, she helps her brother and sister however she can amid the family's ongoing misfortunes.
characters.name: Sunny Baudelaire

characters.description: The greedy, murderous actor determined to steal the Baudelaire fortune, recognizable by his single eyebrow and the eye tattooed on his ankle. A relentless master of disguise, he has already murdered to reach the children's money and escaped capture twice, and the orphans expect him to appear again in some new false identity.
characters.name: Count Olaf

characters.description: The coughing banker who oversees the Baudelaire fortune and keeps relocating the orphans to new guardians. Kind in intention but hopelessly credulous, he rarely believes the children's warnings until it is too late.
characters.name: Mr. Poe

characters.description: The children's new guardian, the widow of a relative, who lives in a rickety house perched on stilts high above Lake Lachrymose. Obsessed with correct grammar, she is also gripped by countless fears, dreading such harmless things as the stove, doorknobs, and the telephone. Timid and easily frightened, she keeps her home cold and cheerless because she is afraid of the radiator, and her nervousness leaves the children feeling far from safe.
characters.name: Aunt Josephine

characters.description: A sinister sailor the family meets near Lake Lachrymose, distinguished by an eye patch and a wooden peg leg, who runs a sailboat rental business. Smooth-talking and eager to ingratiate himself, he showers attention on the fearful Aunt Josephine while treating the children with veiled menace.
characters.name: Captain Sham

recaps.ending: Aunt Josephine, who had gone into hiding to fake her own death, is discovered by the children in Curdled Cave, but her fearfulness dooms her: crossing Lake Lachrymose during Hurricane Herman, the boat is swarmed by the deadly Lachrymose Leeches, and Captain Sham forces the terrified Josephine overboard, where she is killed. Back on shore the Baudelaires expose Captain Sham as Count Olaf by revealing the eye tattoo hidden beneath his fake peg leg, but before Mr. Poe and the others can seize him, Olaf escapes once more. The children have lost another guardian, and their fortune remains the prize Olaf is determined to claim. Mr. Poe takes the orphans back into his care to place them somewhere new, while Count Olaf, exposed but uncaught, slips away to plan his next disguise and his next attempt on the Baudelaires and their money.
recaps.in_short: The Baudelaires are sent to live with fearful, grammar-obsessed Aunt Josephine, whose house teeters on stilts over Lake Lachrymose. In town they meet Captain Sham, a peg-legged sailor they recognize as Count Olaf in disguise, who charms the timid Josephine. Soon Josephine seems to throw herself out her great window into the lake, leaving a note naming Captain Sham as the children's new guardian. Noticing that the note is full of grammatical errors unthinkable for Josephine, the children decode them as a secret message and realize she is alive and hiding in Curdled Cave. During Hurricane Herman they sail across the leech-infested lake and find her, but on the way back the Lachrymose Leeches attack, and Captain Sham forces Josephine into the water to be devoured. On shore the children expose Sham as Olaf by revealing his ankle tattoo, but he escapes yet again. Aunt Josephine is dead, and the orphans are returned to Mr. Poe.

recaps.text: After a fire killed their parents, the Baudelaire orphans, inventor Violet, reader Klaus, and biting baby Sunny, inherited a fortune held in trust and were placed by the banker Mr. Poe with the cruel actor Count Olaf. Olaf tried to steal the money by forcing Violet into a fake marriage, then escaped when she foiled him. The children were next sent to their kind Uncle Monty, a herpetologist, but Olaf followed in disguise as an assistant named Stephano, murdered Monty, and nearly abducted them before the children exposed him; again he escaped, marked always by his single eyebrow and the eye tattooed on his ankle. Having lost two guardians and survived Olaf twice, the orphans are placed by Mr. Poe with yet another relative, fearing that Olaf will appear once more in some new false identity to pursue them and their inheritance.

Mr. Poe delivers the Baudelaires to Aunt Josephine, a nervous widow whose house sits on stilts high over Lake Lachrymose. Josephine is fanatical about correct grammar and terrified of an endless list of ordinary things, from the stove to doorknobs, so her home is cold and comfortless. On a trip into town for groceries the children meet Captain Sham, a sailor with an eye patch and a wooden peg leg who rents out sailboats. Despite his eagerness to befriend Josephine, the children recognize him as Count Olaf in disguise and are alarmed to see him worming his way into their fearful guardian's good graces. They try to warn Josephine and Mr. Poe, but the adults dismiss their suspicions, and the orphans realize that danger has once again followed them to their new home over the water.

Captain Sham continues to charm the anxious Aunt Josephine while the children's warnings go unheeded. Then disaster strikes: Josephine's great window is found shattered, and she appears to have thrown herself out into the lake below, leaving behind a note that makes Captain Sham the children's new guardian. The Baudelaires are grief-stricken but immediately suspicious, because the note is riddled with grammatical mistakes that the grammar-obsessed Josephine would never have made. Studying it closely, they conclude that the errors are deliberate, a hidden message left for them, and that their aunt may not be dead at all. As Captain Sham prepares to take custody of them, the children race to decode the note before they can be handed over to the man they know to be Count Olaf.

The children decipher the intentional errors in the note and discover that Aunt Josephine has faked her death and is hiding in Curdled Cave across Lake Lachrymose. With Hurricane Herman bearing down, they take a sailboat out onto the storm-tossed water, braving wind, waves, and the dreaded Lachrymose Leeches that live in the lake, and reach the cave. There they find Josephine alive but paralyzed by her fears, reluctant to leave her hiding place or to face Captain Sham. The Baudelaires persuade her to come with them, hoping to return safely and expose Sham as Count Olaf, but the crossing back across the churning lake will be far more dangerous than the journey out.

On the return voyage the Lachrymose Leeches, drawn by the fact that Josephine has recently eaten, swarm and attack the boat. Captain Sham appears in his own vessel, and rather than rescue Josephine he forces her into the water, where the leeches devour her. Back on shore, Sham tries to claim the children and their fortune, but the Baudelaires expose him as Count Olaf by revealing the eye tattoo hidden beneath his false peg leg. Confronted at last, Olaf escapes yet again before Mr. Poe can have him arrested, vanishing to plan his next scheme. Aunt Josephine, undone by her own fearfulness, is dead, and the orphans, having lost a third guardian, are returned to Mr. Poe's care to be placed somewhere new while Count Olaf remains free.

characters.description: The narrator: a young man living in an orphanage in the provincial Catenan city of Letens, earning money in an illegal fighting pit to keep the other children there fed. He is fast, disciplined and educated in a way no orphan should be, and he refuses to cede any portion of his Will to a superior, which in this Republic makes him Unranked and gives him no standing, no protection and no prospects. He is hiding who he is. Three years earlier he was Diago, son of the ruling family of the island kingdom of Suus, which the Catenan Republic conquered and whose royal house it destroyed. He is the only survivor, he has told nobody, and his intention is to stay alive and unremarkable. His refusal to cede is both principle and habit, and it is also the most conspicuous thing about him.
characters.name: Vis

characters.description: A senator of the Catenan Republic who takes an interest in Vis and offers him a way out of the orphanage: adoption into the Telimus family, and with it the standing to sit the entrance examinations for the Republic's most prestigious school. The offer is not charity and he does not pretend otherwise. His older brother died years ago at the Catenan Academy, he has never accepted the official account of how, and he wants somebody inside the place who owes him everything and has no prior connection to it. He is single-minded, politically exposed, and running out of other options.
characters.name: Ulciscor Telimus

characters.description: Ulciscor's older brother, a scholar who died at the Catenan Academy several years before the book opens, while investigating the ancient ruins on its grounds. The official account of his death is one Ulciscor has never believed, and everything Ulciscor has done since has been aimed at overturning it.
characters.name: Caeror Telimus

characters.description: A blind woman of the Telimus household who takes charge of preparing Vis for what he is walking into: the Republic's etiquette, its politics, the meaning of its ranks, and the Academy's entrance requirements. She was close to Caeror and knows the Academy from the inside. She is a harder, more exacting and considerably less forgiving teacher than Vis expects, and she has her own reasons for wanting the investigation to succeed.
characters.name: Lanistia

characters.description: The Principalis of the Catenan Academy: charismatic, admired by his students, and one of the most celebrated men in the Republic. He was a friend and colleague of Caeror Telimus and was present when Caeror died. Ulciscor is convinced he is responsible; the Academy regards him as its finest ornament and its guiding intelligence. He takes an interest in the Republic's newest and least connected student that Vis cannot account for.
characters.name: Veridius

characters.description: A student at the Catenan Academy from a family that has lost its standing, which at a school where standing is everything leaves him near the bottom of it. Wry, clever and pessimistic about his own prospects, he is the first person there to treat Vis as something other than an interloper, and he becomes Vis's closest friend.
characters.name: Callidus

characters.description: A student at the Catenan Academy: warm, quick, disarming, and unusually willing to be seen in the company of its newest and least connected arrival. She becomes Vis's closest attachment at the school and the one person there he finds it difficult to stay guarded around, which is a problem for someone whose position depends on being unreadable.
characters.name: Emissa

characters.description: One of the Academy's highest-ranked and most admired students, from a powerful family, genuinely able, and courteous to Vis where others are not. He is what the Republic's system produces when it works as advertised, which makes his easy authority a standing argument for the order Vis has every reason to oppose.
characters.name: Indol

characters.description: A driven, relentlessly competitive student at the Academy from an established family, openly contemptuous of Vis's origins and of the idea that an adopted provincial belongs there at all. She is determined to out-rank him and treats every contest as personal.
characters.name: Aequa

characters.description: A large, taciturn student at the Academy from outside the Republic's heartland, hostile to Vis from their first meeting and unwilling to explain why. Like Vis, he is an outsider at a school that does not disguise what it thinks of outsiders.
characters.name: Eidhin

recaps.ending: Vis reaches the labyrinth beneath the Academy's ruins and completes it, which nobody has done in living memory, and which is what Veridius manoeuvred him toward from the moment he arrived on Solivagus. The arrangements Vis had been living inside collapse around the same event. Emissa's closeness to him was deliberate from the beginning and she had been reporting on him throughout. Ulciscor's real use for him is exposed. His own identity as the last of Suus's royal house stops being a secret he controls. He does get the answer Ulciscor sent him for, what happened to Caeror in the ruins and why, but it arrives attached to a far larger one. The Will that the Republic's citizens cede upward, rank by rank, does not terminate with the Hierarchy's rulers. The entire apparatus of ranks and ceding is a mechanism for gathering that Will and delivering it onward, and the Republic's account of itself as a meritocratic civic order exists to keep that function running unquestioned. Vis ends the book alive and, in the Academy's own terms, successful, but with his cover gone among precisely the people best placed to act on it, obligated to parties he did not choose, and holding knowledge that makes him valuable to everyone and safe with nobody. The Republic he set out merely to survive turns out to be a much larger problem than the one he thought he was hiding from.
recaps.in_short: The Catenan Republic runs on Will: every citizen cedes a share of their own strength and vitality up a strict pyramid of ranks, so that those at the top are far beyond ordinary human capacity and the Republic's machines run on the surplus. Vis, an orphan in the city of Letens, refuses to cede and fights in an illegal pit for money. He is secretly Diago, the last survivor of the royal house of Suus, an island kingdom the Republic destroyed three years earlier. The senator Ulciscor Telimus adopts him in exchange for a task: win a place at the Catenan Academy on Solivagus and investigate the ancient ruins where Ulciscor's brother Caeror died, which Ulciscor believes the Academy's revered Principalis, Veridius, is responsible for. Vis gets in, climbs the school's brutal rankings, makes real friends and one real attachment, and is pressured in turn by Ulciscor, by the rebel Anguis and by Veridius himself. In the end he is betrayed, his secrets come apart, and he completes the labyrinth beneath the ruins, learning that the Will the Republic collects does not stop at its rulers.

recaps.text: The Catenan Republic runs on Will. Every citizen cedes a measured portion of their own strength and vitality to the person above them in a strict pyramid of ranks, so that those near the top are physically and mentally far beyond ordinary human capacity, and the Republic's lights, vehicles and machines run on the surplus. Refusing to cede leaves a person Unranked, with no legal protection and no prospects at all. Vis, a young man in an orphanage in the provincial city of Letens, is Unranked by choice, and fights in an illegal pit to earn money for the children he lives with. He is not what he appears to be. Three years earlier he was Diago, the heir of the island kingdom of Suus, which the Republic conquered and whose royal family it destroyed. He is the only one left, and he has told nobody. His refusal to cede is personal, since the system that took Suus is the system he is being asked to feed, but it is also conspicuous, which is how he comes to the attention of people he would much rather have avoided.

Vis is offered a way out by Ulciscor Telimus, a senator of the Republic, who adopts him into the Telimus family. The price is an assignment. Vis is to win a place at the Catenan Academy, the school on the island of Solivagus that produces the Republic's rulers, and once inside, investigate the ancient ruins on its grounds. Ulciscor's brother Caeror died there years ago; Ulciscor believes the Academy's Principalis, Veridius, killed him, and that whatever Caeror found in the ruins is the reason. Vis accepts, because the arrangement gives him a name, a family and a legitimate reason to be somewhere he could otherwise never reach. He is trained for the entrance examinations and for Catenan society by Lanistia, a blind woman of Ulciscor's household who knew Caeror well, and he has to conceal both his origins and the fact that he still cedes nothing to anyone.

Vis's preparation is compressed and punishing, and the Academy's selection process is designed to exclude anyone without either a pedigree or exceptional ability. He gets in, and discovers that his position is worse than he anticipated. At a school where standing is everything, the adopted son of a minor senatorial house has almost none, and the internal rankings are contested continuously rather than settled once. He also has to manage the central lie of his situation, since the Academy assumes its students cede and Vis cannot. The first part of the book closes with him arriving on Solivagus, committed to an investigation he does not believe in, on behalf of a man he does not trust, in a place where being noticed at all is dangerous for him.

At the Academy Vis begins climbing the class rankings, which are decided by public contests of strategy, combat and scholarship, and learns quickly that ability alone will not carry him: the school's politics run on family, patronage and the shared assumption that the Republic's hierarchy is natural and correct. He acquires the beginnings of a circle. Callidus, a sardonic student from a fallen family, is the first to treat him as a person. Emissa is unaccountably willing to be seen with him. The relentless Aequa and the highly ranked Indol regard him as an intruder, and Eidhin is hostile for reasons of his own. Vis also starts looking, cautiously, at the ruins and at Veridius, who is admired by the entire school and who takes an interest in Vis that Vis cannot explain.

Vis's two lives begin pulling against each other. Ulciscor presses for progress on the ruins, the Academy demands total commitment to its rankings, and the Anguis, the rebel organisation that opposes the Hierarchy and is hunted by it, makes contact and applies pressure of its own that Vis can neither accept nor safely refuse. He learns that the ruins on Solivagus contain a labyrinth of pre-Republic origin, that Caeror and Veridius explored it together, that Caeror died inside it, and that Veridius has never stopped trying to reach its end. Vis's own past intrudes as well: people capable of recognising Diago of Suus exist, and the Republic's interest in Suus did not finish with the conquest.

Vis rises far enough in the Academy's rankings to be a contender rather than a curiosity, which makes him a target for everyone who assumed the top places were already spoken for. He gets into the ruins, confirms that the labyrinth is real and that it is a structure with rules rather than a collapsed building, and satisfies himself that Veridius's interest in it is not antiquarian. His relationships complicate the assignment badly: Callidus is a friend rather than an asset, and his attachment to Emissa is genuine, which is a liability for someone whose safety depends on being unreadable. The second part of the book ends with Vis committed to the Academy's final competition, the Iudicium, and with the question of what Caeror actually found no longer an academic one.

The Iudicium is run as a public contest and Vis is at the centre of it. The competition works against him as much as for him: what he can do without ceding is difficult to explain innocently, and the further he advances the more visible he becomes to exactly the people he has spent three years avoiding. Pressure arrives from every direction at once, from Ulciscor's demands, from the Anguis, from the Academy's own factions, and from Veridius, whose attention on him has become impossible to write off as coincidence. People close to Vis are hurt as a direct consequence of his being there, and the cost of Ulciscor's investigation stops being something Vis can treat as abstract.

The last stretch runs as a cascade. Vis is betrayed by someone he had come to depend on: Emissa was placed close to him deliberately and had been reporting on him from the start, and the deceptions on every side come apart together. He goes into the labyrinth beneath the Academy's ruins and completes it, which nobody has managed in living memory and which is what Veridius wanted from him all along. What he finds there answers Ulciscor's question about how and why Caeror died, and a much larger question besides. The Will that the Republic's citizens cede upward does not stop at the top of the Hierarchy. The whole structure of ranks and ceding exists to gather that Will and deliver it onward, and the Republic's account of itself as a civic order that rewards merit is the cover for that function. Vis ends the book alive and, in the Academy's terms, successful, but with his cover destroyed among the people best able to act on it, bound to parties he did not choose, and holding knowledge that makes him valuable to everyone and safe with no one.

characters.description: A quiet, good-hearted animal who abandons his spring cleaning and discovers life beyond his underground home. New to boats and the wider countryside, he approaches each adventure with wonder and forms a close friendship with Rat.
characters.name: Mole

characters.description: A sociable water vole devoted to the river and to boating. He welcomes Mole into his settled riverside life, teaches him to handle a boat, and proves a loyal, practical friend when trouble arises.
characters.name: Rat

characters.description: The wealthy owner of Toad Hall, exuberant, vain, and forever consumed by a new craze. When Mole and Rat visit, he has transferred his enthusiasm from boating to a brightly painted caravan and insists that his friends join him on the road.
characters.name: Toad

characters.description: A formidable and private resident of the Wild Wood whom Rat regards as a dependable friend. He dislikes society and formal calls, but his authority, hospitality, and deep knowledge of the countryside make him a powerful ally.
characters.name: Badger

characters.description: A confident riverbank neighbor and friend of Rat. He is at home in the water and among the local animals, and his family is part of the close community Mole begins to know.
characters.name: Otter

characters.description: Otter's young son, whose unexplained absence sends the riverbank animals searching through the night.
characters.name: Portly

aliases: The Piper at the Gates of Dawn
characters.description: A mysterious horned guardian whom Rat and Mole encounter at daybreak during their search for Portly. His music fills them with awe and offers protection to a lost child of the countryside.
characters.name: Pan

characters.description: A compassionate young woman who helps oversee the imprisoned Toad. Amused by his dramatic misery, she devises a disguise that gives him a chance to escape.
characters.name: The Gaoler's Daughter

characters.description: A seasoned traveler who visits Rat by the river and describes long journeys, distant ports, and a life guided by migration. His stories awaken in Rat a sudden longing to leave home.
characters.name: The Sea Rat

characters.description: A working woman carrying cargo along the canal who initially gives the disguised Toad food and passage. She assumes he can perform the household work his costume suggests.
characters.name: The Barge-woman

characters.description: The leader of the Wild Wood animals who have occupied Toad Hall. He commands the defenders of the house and presides over their victory celebrations.
characters.name: The Chief Weasel

recaps.ending: Badger leads Rat, Mole, and Toad through a secret tunnel into Toad Hall while the weasels and stoats are holding a banquet. The friends surprise the occupiers and drive them from the house. Toad wants to turn his return into a public spectacle, but the others restrain him and organize a modest celebration. He sends gifts and apologies to people he wronged during his escape and appears to have become humbler and more considerate. Although his friends remain alert for another burst of vanity, Toad Hall is restored, the four companions are honored locally, and peaceful life on the riverbank resumes.
recaps.in_short: Mole leaves his underground home and discovers the river with Rat, whose friendship draws him into a changing year of picnics, journeys, danger, and homecoming. They meet the impulsive Toad, whose latest obsession becomes motorcars. After repeated crashes and ignored warnings, Toad steals a car, is imprisoned, escapes in disguise, and makes a chaotic journey home. Rat and Mole also survive the Wild Wood, befriend the reclusive Badger, recover Mole's neglected home, and help Otter find his missing son. When Toad returns, he learns that weasels and stoats have seized Toad Hall. Badger, Rat, and Mole guide him through a hidden passage, and the friends expel the intruders. Toad accepts their efforts to curb his vanity, makes amends for some of his behavior, and is restored to his home and community.

recaps.text: Mole tires of cleaning his underground home and bursts into the spring sunshine. At the river he meets Rat, who introduces him to boating, picnics, and the pleasures of riverside life. Mole's first attempt to manage the boat ends with him in the water, but Rat rescues him and invites him to stay. The friends later visit wealthy Toad at Toad Hall. Toad has abandoned his previous hobbies for a horse-drawn caravan and persuades them to travel with him. Their excursion ends when a speeding motorcar frightens the horse and wrecks the caravan. Instead of being discouraged, Toad becomes instantly fascinated by motorcars and forgets the caravan entirely.

Mole grows curious about the Wild Wood and enters it alone during winter. The unfamiliar forest becomes frightening after dark, and its hostile inhabitants drive him into hiding. Rat follows to find him, but snow covers their way home. They discover a door belonging to Badger, Rat's respected but unsociable friend. Badger gives them warmth, food, and shelter in his extensive underground home. He listens to their concerns about Toad, whose motorcar obsession has already caused repeated crashes and legal trouble, and agrees that they must intervene. Badger then guides Mole and Rat safely through underground passages to the edge of the Wild Wood, returning them to their own familiar country.

On a winter walk, Mole catches the scent of his old home and quietly longs to see it again. Rat recognizes his distress and helps reopen and provision Mole End, where they host field mice singing seasonal songs. In spring, Badger confronts Toad about his dangerous driving. Toad promises to reform but soon escapes Rat's supervision. When an unattended motorcar appears outside an inn, he steals it and is arrested. His courtroom boasting and insults worsen the case, and he receives a long prison sentence. His friends are unable to prevent his removal, leaving Toad confined and Toad Hall without its owner.

Otter's young son Portly disappears, and Rat and Mole search the river through the night. Near dawn they hear unearthly music and encounter the protective figure Pan, with Portly sleeping safely beside him. The friends return the child to his father, retaining only a fading sense of wonder. In prison, Toad wins the sympathy of the gaoler's daughter. She disguises him as a washerwoman and helps him escape. Still wearing the disguise, Toad buys passage on a train, but the authorities pursue him. The engine driver helps him evade them, and Toad leaps from the train into the woods, free but far from home.

A visiting Sea Rat fills Rat's imagination with accounts of migration and distant coasts. Rat nearly abandons the river, but Mole recognizes the spell of the traveler's stories and gently brings him back to himself. Meanwhile, the fugitive Toad continues home in his washerwoman disguise. A barge-woman feeds him and offers him a ride, then throws him into the canal when his lack of washing skill exposes him. Toad retaliates by stealing her horse, later sells it, and flags down a motorcar. The car belongs to the people whose vehicle he earlier stole. Allowed to drive before they recognize him, he loses control, reveals himself, and lands in the water again. At last he reaches the river, where Rat pulls him into safety.

Rat tells Toad that weasels and stoats from the Wild Wood have occupied Toad Hall. Toad initially tries to retake it alone and is driven off. Badger and Mole join them, and Badger reveals a secret tunnel leading beneath the house. While the occupiers hold a banquet, the four friends enter through the passage, surprise them, and clear the Hall. Toad imagines an elaborate celebration of his own glory, but his friends insist on a restrained dinner and make him send apologies and gifts to people he mistreated. He behaves with unusual modesty at the gathering and acknowledges the friends who restored him. Toad Hall returns to its owner, and Badger, Rat, Mole, and Toad settle back into an honored place in the local community.

characters.description: A classless city runner known locally as the Windrunner. An independent wind gathers around her and assists her movement as she takes dangerous work near Raismelt.
characters.name: Ryoka Griffin

characters.description: A sickly information broker in Raismelt who secretly examines letters carried by runners. She keeps her true nature hidden at the inn where she lives.
characters.name: Young vampire

characters.description: A badly injured member of the Pithfire Hounds. Ryoka carries him to safety during an emergency delivery after bringing the trapped adventurers the potions they need, and his survival helps establish her as a dependable runner.
characters.name: Lamont

characters.description: The innkeeper of the Wandering Inn, a refuge for guests of many species. Her unusual inn, its magical door, and the household gathered around it remain central to her life near Liscor.
characters.name: Erin Solstice

characters.description: Erin's capable inn manager and Mrsha's guardian. She helps sustain the Wandering Inn as a home and shares responsibility for the young Gnoll.
characters.name: Lyonette

characters.description: A young mute Gnoll in the care of Erin and Lyonette. Recovering from earlier trauma, she is part of the close household formed around the Wandering Inn.
characters.name: Mrsha

characters.description: A member of Erin's chosen family who has a permanent home at the Wandering Inn.
characters.name: Bird

characters.description: A wounded Redfang Goblin bard and resident of the Wandering Inn.
characters.name: Numbtongue

characters.description: A fallen Goblin who took part in the defense of Liscor.
characters.name: Pyrite

characters.description: A Stitch Person alchemist based in Selim whose cloth body can be taken apart and repaired. Her business connection to the inn's magical door brings her to check on Erin while the inn is closed by grief.
characters.name: Octavia

characters.description: A Drake Wall Lord and established ally in Liscor.
characters.name: Ilvriss

characters.description: The half-elf leader of the Horns of Hammerad. She has unresolved business with the team's imprisoned former captain and the dungeon beneath Liscor.
characters.name: Ceria Springwalker

characters.description: The imprisoned former captain of Ceria's team. Disabled and awaiting judgment, he remains connected to the dungeon disaster and to the companions whose deaths and unfinished work continue to weigh on the Horns.
characters.name: Calruz

characters.description: Liscor's strategist.
characters.name: Olesm

characters.description: The necromancer formerly behind the Goblin Lord and a concealed danger to the Drake cities.
characters.name: Az'kerash

characters.description: A Japanese arrival from Earth and negotiator for the United Nations Company. His language skill and local contacts help hold together a precarious refuge made up of other Earth arrivals, former mercenaries, and local allies.
characters.name: Kenjiro Murata

characters.description: The Australian captain of the Bush Rangers, a silver-rank team using camouflage, traps, crossbows, and poisoned bolts. He seeks safer paid work for the United Nations Company while he and his teammates carry the effects of earlier battles.
characters.name: Dally

characters.description: A Swedish member of the Bush Rangers who specializes in camouflage. She joined the team after surviving apart from its original members.
characters.name: Siri

characters.description: An Australian aspiring writer who proposed supporting the United Nations Company by selling her romance fiction. She disappeared without a known resolution, leaving Dally with her unfinished work.
characters.name: Caroline

characters.description: A Dullahan adventurer who commands the silver-rank Rustless Guard. A dispute over an assignment ends when Dally offers her an honorable apology and a drink.
characters.name: Eldemar

characters.description: An Italian physician whose medicine is indispensable to the United Nations Company. Known locally as the Last Light of Boleros, she wants her work to support the group, though her value and limited protection make battlefield service especially dangerous.
characters.name: Geneva Scala

characters.description: The United Nations Company's treasurer and an inventive designer. She manages the group's dwindling shared funds, improves the Bush Rangers' crossbows, and looks for practical ways to preserve equipment brought from Earth.
characters.name: Paige

characters.description: A South African Olympic rowing hopeful who has turned his abilities toward courier work. He plans to earn income for the United Nations Company by carrying messages over water in a canoe.
characters.name: Luan

characters.description: An Italian arrival from Earth found malnourished after hiding from violent attackers. Her diabetes becomes an immediate danger because she has no insulin, leaving the rescuers to stabilize her until Geneva returns.
characters.name: Diana

characters.description: A traumatized New Zealand arrival from Earth rescued with three Italian survivors. He gives the Bush Rangers their first account of other Earth humans attacking the group with two young centaurs.
characters.name: Blake

characters.description: A distinct being sharing Geneva's living body. Able to control parts of that body with precision, the self-ed assists her medical work directly while remaining a separate presence with medical uncertainties of its own.
characters.name: Self-ed

characters.description: Geneva's nurse and surgical assistant. She supports the doctor's medical research and helps during emergency treatment, including a difficult operation to save a centaur mother and her child.
characters.name: Aiko

characters.description: A Minotaur planner who covertly hires Luan for a time-sensitive future delivery connected to the Titan's recurring game.
characters.name: Vanaz

characters.description: The Titan and head of the Forgotten Wing Company. Presented with unfamiliar nonmagical devices and reports about the United Nations Company, he privately concludes that people from another world are probably involved and begins an encrypted inquiry.
characters.name: Niers Astoragon

characters.description: A bee bonded to Lyonette and protective of her and Mrsha. It serves as a messenger and uses sustained flame-powered flight to outlast an attacking swarm's queen and claim territory.
characters.name: Lyonette's ashfire bee

characters.description: Liscor's Watch captain. She accepts Lyonette's plan to repay damage from earlier crimes and keeps the confiscated artifacts until the agreed fine is paid.
characters.name: Zevara

characters.description: A Gnoll bartender who owns Tails and Scales with his wife, Lassica. He comforts Erin and helps organize opposition to a concealed visitor fee.
characters.name: Rufelt

characters.description: A Drake chef who owns Tails and Scales with her husband, Rufelt. She comforts Erin and helps organize opposition to a concealed visitor fee.
characters.name: Lassica

characters.description: A skilled and expensive Drake scribe in Liscor. Olesm hires her to reproduce his strategy and chess publication, making her craft part of the effort to preserve and distribute the city's hard-won lessons.
characters.name: Ressa

characters.description: The King of Destruction and ruler of Rhyme. He enters Germina's succession as its foreign witness, offers its reborn ruler protected self-rule within his realm, and then takes Helios after its queen abdicates.
characters.name: Flos

characters.description: Flos's steward and left hand, responsible for turning conquest into administration. He prepares control arrangements for Germina and Helios and receives a desert clan whose young blacksmith has sworn to forge Flos an exceptional weapon.
characters.name: Orthenon

characters.description: An Earth-born teenage mage chosen as Flos's companion. Training under Rhyme's formidable vassals, he learns to cast Farsight without a staff while becoming involved with the arrival of a desert clan and its demanding oath.
characters.name: Trey

characters.description: An independent ruler formerly associated with Flos. At a neutral gathering of southern powers, she refuses to join opposition to him and commits her country to honoring his peace declaration and the return of those who claim his allegiance.
characters.name: Empress of Beasts

characters.description: The martial champion of a neutral sanctuary. The champion enforces its rules, refuses political killing, and ends a violent clash among visiting rulers without taking a life.
characters.name: Neutral sanctuary champion

characters.description: A Drake secretary who manages a neutral sanctuary. She secretly uses her document-copying ability to preserve the Emperor of Sands' proposal.
characters.name: Neutral sanctuary secretary

characters.description: A former mercenary captain allied with the United Nations Company. He urges the group to seek paid contracts, while recognizing that Geneva is too valuable and too poorly protected to serve safely as a battlefield doctor.
characters.name: Qualet

characters.description: A child incarnation who inherits Germina's cuirass office and memories while remaining a distinct person. As Germina's ruler, she accepts Flos's protection and an alliance that preserves her territory's self-rule within Rhyme.
characters.name: Reborn cuirass of Germina

characters.description: The only remaining smith in her desert clan able to work its rare metal. She arrives in Rhyme under an oath to forge Flos an exceptional weapon and bears responsibility for preserving the craft taught by her father.
characters.name: Desert-clan blacksmith

characters.description: A Lizardfolk sorcerer allied with the United Nations Company. After losing a foot in battle, she received a peg leg made by Geneva.
characters.name: Kexa

characters.description: A half-Gazer who puts Trey through demanding magical training. Under her instruction, he learns to cast Farsight without a staff.
characters.name: Ghazi

characters.description: The twin of Trey, from whom she has grown distant after a disagreement. They resume warmer contact and agree to speak privately as they begin repairing their relationship.
characters.name: Therese

recaps.ending:
The numbered story ends with Flos's peace declaration reshaping southern politics. Some rulers accept the demand to release his former subjects rather than risk war, while the Empress of Beasts refuses to join resistance against him. Her position leaves her isolated, and nine nations declare war on her country after a tense summit. The Emperor of Sands' copied proposal remains unexplained.

Elsewhere, Ryoka remains free and trusted by the concealed vampire family, whose illness and search for Rose, Imani, and Joseph remain unresolved. Lyonette runs the reopened Wandering Inn, Mrsha studies signs and magic, and Numbtongue holds Pyrite's memories, valuable mana stones, and unstable magicore. Ilvriss quietly investigates Az'kerash. The United Nations Company has new allies and medical prospects but still faces financial pressure, hostile Earth arrivals, fading memories, and Niers's attention. In the material following the numbered chapters, the long-range door proves too costly for regular travel, several visiting teams depart, and Ceria's Horns stay behind with the goal of reaching gold rank. The dungeon and Calruz's fate remain open.
recaps.in_short: Ryoka earns the name Windrunner through dangerous deliveries, befriends a hidden family of living vampires, and agrees to protect their secret while they search for missing Earth arrivals. In Liscor, Erin reopens her inn after the Goblins' deaths, recognizes Numbtongue as family, and leaves Lyonette to manage their growing home. Numbtongue inherits Pyrite's memories and hazardous mining knowledge. The United Nations Company rescues stranded Earth arrivals and wins allies through adventuring and Geneva's medicine, but remains poor, traumatized, and threatened by hostile Earth humans, fading memories, and Niers's secret inquiry. Ilvriss confirms that Az'kerash lives and begins a covert investigation. Flos adds Germina and Helios to Rhyme, expands weapons production, and demands safe passage for anyone claiming his allegiance. Nine nations then declare war on the Empress of Beasts. Afterward, visiting adventuring teams leave Erin's inn, while Ceria's Horns remain and resolve to pursue gold rank.

recaps.text: Previously: Erin Solstice established the Wandering Inn near Liscor as a refuge whose guests cross ordinary boundaries of species and allegiance. Lyonette helps run the inn and care for Mrsha, a young mute Gnoll, while Redfang Goblins including Numbtongue became part of its community. The struggle around Liscor ended with Goblins dying in the city's defense, leaving Erin and the survivors in grief. Ceria Springwalker leads the rebuilt Horns of Hammerad, but the team's former captain Calruz remains imprisoned after the dungeon disaster. Wall Lord Ilvriss has become an ally in Liscor, while the necromancer Az'kerash remains a concealed threat. Elsewhere, Earth arrivals have been scattered across the world. Ryoka Griffin works as a classless runner, and a mixed group of other arrivals and local allies has begun forming the United Nations Company.

Ryoka's northern work earns her the name Windrunner. She rescues the trapped Pithfire Hounds, then discovers that a Raismelt broker belongs to a hidden family of living vampires. The family cannot compel her silence, but she promises it freely after learning that they survive on animal blood and suffer a worsening inherited illness or curse. Ryoka and the young vampire become friends, and Ryoka asks her to search for Rose, Imani, and Joseph.

At the Wandering Inn, Erin's grief initially shuts out Liscor. Numbtongue openly challenges the city's treatment of the Goblins who defended it, buries Pyrite, and begins receiving the dead Goblin's memories. Erin names Lyonette, Mrsha, Numbtongue, and Bird as family, reopens the inn, and prepares to travel while Lyonette takes charge. Numbtongue gains public recognition as an adventurer and chooses the inn as his home.

The United Nations Company is nearly out of money. Dally's Bush Rangers become its main adventuring income, rescue four starving Earth arrivals, and learn that other Earth humans attacked them. Geneva returns to treat the newcomers. When giant serpents escape a dungeon, Dally delays them and Ken mobilizes local forces. Geneva then saves a centaur mother and child through emergency surgery. These successes win goodwill and an alliance with the indebted Rustless Guard, but the company remains financially fragile.

The United Nations Company searches for a sustainable future. Geneva considers a clinic and develops uncertain antibacterial treatment, while Paige confirms she can make gunpowder and the group secretly plans nonmagical grenades. Aiko and Luan recognize that Earthworlders are losing memories of their families. Luan tattoos his wife and son's names on his arm, continues earning money as a water courier, and accepts a covert delivery connected to the Titan's recurring game. Niers Astoragon examines Earth devices, concludes that another world's people are present, and opens a private investigation.

Lyonette expands her control of the Wandering Inn, negotiates restitution for her old crimes, teaches Mrsha more signs, and strengthens her bond with an ashfire bee. Erin visits another walled city through the magical door, where she finds a concealed visitor fee and a law that would kill Numbtongue if he entered. Sympathetic tradespeople begin challenging the fee. Numbtongue uses Pyrite's inherited mining knowledge to find mana stone and magicore, but his music transforms the material into an unstable electrical hazard.

Ceria visits Calruz in prison. He accepts responsibility for his actions and continues mapping the dungeon while expecting execution.

Flos enters Germina's succession ritual as the required foreign witness and protects its newly reborn child ruler. She accepts self-rule within Rhyme, and they agree to stop creating new child assassins. Flos then takes Helios after its queen abdicates, offering her son a chance to earn the kingdom's restoration through service. These settlements enlarge Rhyme but leave both territories unstable.

A desert clan reaches Rhyme under Orthenon's protection. Its young blacksmith proves her rare purification craft by forging a superior individual blade. Flos preserves the resident master smith's position because his work can equip an army, while commissioning the clan for exceptional weapons. He adopts a growth edict despite the pressure it will place on resources, judges that a coalition is his chief danger, and sends a continent-wide peace ultimatum. He promises not to attack states that leave him and his subjects alone, but demands safe release and passage for anyone who claims allegiance to him.

The ultimatum forces rulers to choose between losing experienced subjects and provoking Flos. At a neutral southern sanctuary, the Empress of Beasts refuses to join an anti-Flos alignment and agrees to honor his demand. The sanctuary's champion ends a violent confrontation without killing anyone. Its secretary secretly copies a proposal from the Emperor of Sands, but the contents remain unknown. The next day, nine southern nations declare war on the Empress of Beasts' country, opening a new conflict as Flos's expanding realm continues to prepare for wider war.
